explanations.answer: The godly and the faithful have vanished
explanations.explanation: That's the whole reason David cries out. He says "…the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men." He doesn't open with small talk. He opens with "Help, O LORD…" and then lays out the trouble.

explanations.answer: His enemies have surrounded the city
explanations.explanation: No army shows up in this psalm, friend. David's trouble is about people. He says "…the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men." I think that's a different kind of lonely than a city under siege.

explanations.answer: The rain has stopped across the land
explanations.explanation: David never mentions rain or any weather. His complaint is about people: "…the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men." He says it to the LORD right after crying "Help." Nobody is checking the sky in this psalm.

David says "They lie to one another…" and that's right alongside the flattering lips and the double heart. The words sound sweet, but the heart behind them isn't matching. I think that's what makes a double heart so hard to spot.
Not quite, friend. David says "They lie to one another; they speak with flattering lips and a double heart." Listening isn't in that line. What David names is the lying and the flattering lips.
Fun guess, and this psalm is for the choirmaster, so a song isn't out of place. But David says "They lie to one another…" Singing isn't what he names. The lying is.
David prays, "May the LORD cut off all flattering lips and every boastful tongue." Notice he brings it to the LORD in prayer. He asks the LORD to do the cutting off.

That's a kind guess, friend, but it's not what David asks here. His words are "May the LORD cut off all flattering lips and every boastful tongue." The flattering lips and the boastful tongues are the ones he names.

Not this time. David prays, "May the LORD cut off all flattering lips and every boastful tongue." Blessing flattering lips would be like giving a bigger megaphone to the loudest person at the party. David asks for the opposite.
They say, "With our tongues we will prevail." That's the boast, plain and simple. It comes right after David prays about flattering lips and every boastful tongue.
No swords in this boast, friend. They say, "With our tongues we will prevail." Their weapon is talk, and they're proud of it.
Chariots never roll into this psalm. The smooth talkers say, "With our tongues we will prevail." The only equipment they're counting on is already in their mouths.
Careful, this one flips it around. These folks say, "We own our lips—who can be our master?" That's the opposite of answering to the LORD. They're saying nobody is over them at all.
Right, because they say the opposite. Their words are "We own our lips—who can be our master?" They're asking who could possibly be their master. The very next verse is the LORD speaking.

Yes, and it's a big moment. After the smooth talkers finish bragging, the LORD says, "…I will now arise…" in verse 5. The psalm has been David talking, and then the LORD speaks for Himself. Those boasters said nobody could be their master, and then the LORD speaks.
It's true, friend. In verse 5 the LORD speaks for Himself, and He says, "…I will now arise…" The LORD doesn't stay quiet in this psalm. After all that boasting, He speaks up in His own voice.
The LORD says, "For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise…" He hears the groaning. He also says, "I will bring safety to him who yearns."

Not this one, friend. The LORD says, "For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise…" The oppressed and the needy are the ones He names. The boasters were the ones talking back in verse 4.
No kings or mighty ones are named here. The LORD says, "For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise…" He's rising for the people who are hurting and in need.
David says, "The words of the LORD are flawless, like silver refined in a furnace…" Flawless means nothing is wrong with them. After a whole psalm about slippery, lying words, that's a big contrast.
Not hidden, friend. David says, "The words of the LORD are flawless, like silver refined in a furnace…" He's praising how pure they are, and he doesn't say a word about them being tucked away.

David doesn't mention how old the words are. He says, "The words of the LORD are flawless, like silver refined in a furnace…" The picture he gives is refined silver, and the word he picks is flawless.

explanations.answer: Keep us and guard us forever
explanations.explanation: David says, "You, O LORD, will keep us; You will forever guard us from this generation." He's talking right to the LORD now. The crowd around him is lying and boasting, but his hope is in the One who keeps and guards.

explanations.answer: Send us off to the mountains
explanations.explanation: No mountain trip in this psalm. David says, "You, O LORD, will keep us; You will forever guard us from this generation." Mountains aren't in his words. He says the LORD will keep and guard.
David doesn't say that. His words are "You, O LORD, will keep us; You will forever guard us from this generation." He says the LORD will keep and guard, and he says nothing about being left alone.

Look at that last line again. David ends with "The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men." He says the wicked wander freely, not that they've been driven away. That's where the psalm ends.

Right, the last line says the opposite. David ends with "The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men." The wicked are still out there. He sings the whole psalm straight, and he doesn't tie the ending up with a bow.
